questions.question: Which of the following statements about a Java class definition is true?
options: A .java file may contain several public top‑level classes, each with its own name.
A class definition allocates memory for its instance fields once, and all objects share the same copy.
Any class that contains a method can be executed directly from the command line without a main method.
A class definition is only a blueprint; it does not allocate storage for instance fields until an object is created with the new operator.
questions.explanation: A class in Java merely describes the shape of objects. No memory for instance variables is allocated when the class is compiled; each time new is used a separate object is created on the heap with its own copies of the fields. Execution of a program still requires a public static void main method, and a source file may contain at most one public top‑level class whose name must match the filename. Therefore the third statement correctly reflects the purpose of a class definition.

questions.question: Which statement about Java constructors is correct?
options: All constructors defined in a superclass are automatically available in a subclass without any additional code.
A constructor is called automatically when the new operator creates an object, and its purpose is to initialize the object's fields.
The constructor itself allocates memory on the heap for the new object before its body runs.
A constructor can be invoked on an existing object reference like a regular method, e.g., obj.MyClass().
questions.explanation: When the new operator is used, it first allocates memory for the object, then immediately invokes the appropriate constructor to initialize the object's fields. Constructors are not called like ordinary methods on existing objects, they do not allocate memory themselves, and they are not inherited by subclasses.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the effect of omitting an access modifier (default access) on a class member in Java?
options: It restricts access to classes that are defined in the same package as the declaring class.
It grants access to any class in any package, effectively acting like public.
It allows subclasses in other packages to inherit the member, but not other classes in the same package.
It can be used on top‑level classes to hide them from other packages, similar to the protected modifier.
questions.explanation: When no access modifier is specified, the member receives package‑private (default) access. This means only classes that reside in the exact same package as the declaring class can see the member. It is not public, it does not become visible to subclasses in different packages, and top‑level classes cannot be declared protected or private.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of abstraction in object-oriented design?
options: Abstraction is only about making fields private.
Abstraction and encapsulation are the same; both hide internal details.
Abstraction requires the abstract keyword to be used.
Abstraction focuses on exposing essential behavior while hiding implementation details.
questions.explanation: The correct answer explains that abstraction is about exposing the essential behavior of a type and hiding the incidental implementation details. The other options incorrectly state that abstraction requires the abstract keyword, equate abstraction with encapsulation, or limit it to private fields.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about default methods in Java interfaces is true?
options: An interface can provide default implementations for equals(), hashCode(), or toString().
An interface method with a body is automatically a default method without writing the default keyword.
Default methods can declare and mutate interface-level instance fields.
A default method must be marked with default; otherwise the compiler rejects it.
questions.explanation: In Java, a method in an interface that has a body must be explicitly declared with the default keyword; otherwise the compiler will reject it. The other statements reflect common misconceptions: assuming the keyword is optional, believing default methods can access instance fields of an interface, or thinking interfaces can override Object methods with default implementations.

options: Compilation fails because DataCorruptException is a checked exception and must be declared or caught.
Corruption detected
The program prints nothing because unchecked exceptions are ignored by the JVM at runtime.
Compilation fails because the compiler treats all exceptions as checked and requires a throws clause.
questions.explanation: DataCorruptException extends RuntimeException, making it an unchecked exception. Therefore the process() method does not need a throws declaration, and the catch block handles the thrown instance, printing its message "Corruption detected". Unchecked exceptions are still thrown at runtime, and the program compiles and runs successfully.

questions.question: Which statement about default values of fields and variables in Java is correct?
options: Local primitive variables are given a default value of zero when a method begins.
Numeric instance fields contain indeterminate values until explicitly assigned.
Instance boolean fields are automatically initialized to false.
Instance boolean fields are automatically initialized to true.
questions.explanation: Java guarantees that all instance (and static) fields are zero‑initialized before any constructor or initializer runs. Booleans default to false, numeric types default to 0 (or 0.0, '\u0000'), and reference types default to null. This automatic initialization applies only to fields; local variables inside methods are not given default values and must be explicitly assigned before use.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the Java default (no‑argument) constructor is correct?
options: The compiler always generates a no‑argument constructor for every class, even if the class already defines one or more constructors.
A class that contains a blank final instance field can rely on the compiler‑generated default constructor to compile without errors.
When a class explicitly declares a zero‑argument constructor, that constructor is the default constructor supplied by the compiler.
The compiler supplies a no‑argument constructor only when the class declares no constructors at all.
questions.explanation: The Java language specification states that a default constructor is created by the compiler only if the class has no explicit constructor declarations. If any constructor (including a no‑argument one) is written, the compiler does not generate a default constructor. Therefore, the fourth option accurately describes the rule, while the other three reflect common misconceptions.

options: The compiler prefers the int version over the double version because primitive widening is chosen before boxing.
There is no compile error; the code compiles and runs without producing any output.
The compiler reports: method compute(int) is already defined; return type alone cannot be used to overload a method.
The two methods differ only by their throws clauses, which is not allowed for overloading.
questions.explanation: In Java the method signature consists of the method name and its parameter types; the return type is not part of the signature. Therefore declaring two methods with identical parameter lists but different return types causes a compile‑time error: 'method compute(int) is already defined'. The other statements describe unrelated misconceptions or are simply incorrect.

questions.question: Which statement best describes how inheritance works in Java?
options: A subclass does not contain any of the private fields declared in its superclass, so those fields are not part of the subclass’s object layout.
You should use inheritance whenever a class needs to reuse functionality from another class, even if there is no true “is‑a” relationship.
Inheritance works by copying all the superclass’s methods and fields into the subclass’s bytecode, so the subclass has its own independent copies.
When a class extends another, the subclass automatically has access to the superclass’s accessible members, and the JVM links them at runtime without duplicating the superclass code.
questions.explanation: Extending a class creates an is‑a relationship; the subclass inherits the accessible (public/protected) members of the superclass. The JVM resolves method calls and field accesses through the class hierarchy, so no code is copied into the subclass bytecode. The first option is wrong because inheritance does not duplicate code. The second option misapplies inheritance to any reuse scenario, ignoring the need for a true subtype relationship. The fourth option is incorrect because a subclass object does contain the superclass’s private fields; they are simply not directly accessible by name.

options: The call a.speak() invokes Dog's overriding method, while the field access a.name yields the value from Animal because fields are not polymorphic.
The private method whisper() in Animal can be overridden in Dog and would be called by a.whisper() at runtime.
Both the method call and the field access are resolved using the reference type Animal, so a.speak() prints "Generic animal" and a.name is "animal".
Both the method call and the field access are resolved using the runtime type Dog, so a.speak() prints "Woof" and a.name is "dog".
questions.explanation: Method dispatch in Java is dynamic: the actual object is a Dog, so the overridden speak() runs and prints "Woof". Field access is static: the compiler uses the declared type Animal, therefore a.name refers to Animal.name and prints "animal". Private methods cannot be overridden, so they are bound at compile time and are not accessible via the reference.

options: BD
DB
D
B
questions.explanation: When a Derived object is instantiated, the compiler automatically inserts a call to super() as the first statement of Derived's constructor. Thus the Base constructor runs first, printing "B", followed by the Derived constructor printing "D". The combined output is "BD". The option "D" reflects the misconception that the superclass constructor is not automatically invoked.
